## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92844.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92844.3.sa2)

Zhao et al., focus on mechanisms through which cells convert from epithelium to mesenchyme and become migratory. This phenomenon of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) occurs during both embryonic development and cancer progression. During cancer progression, EMT seemingly includes cells at intermediate states as defined by the combinatorial expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers. But the importance of these markers and the role of these intermediate states remains unclear. Moreover, whether EMT during development also involves equivalent intermediate cell states is not known. To address this gap in knowledge, the authors devise a strategy to identify and characterize changes that an embryonic population of cells called the cranial neural crest undergo as they delaminate from the neuroepithelium and become a highly migratory population of mesenchymal cells that ultimately give rise to a broad range of derivatives.

To isolate and study the neural crest, the authors use embryos collected at E8.5 from two transgenic mouse lines. Wnt1-Cre;RosaeYFP labels Wnt1-positive neuroepithelial cells in the dorsolateral neural plate, which includes pre-migratory neural crest that reside in the dorsal neuroectoderm and neural plate border before induction (as well as some other lineages). Mef2c-F10N-LacZ leverages a neural crest cell-specific enhancer of Mef2c to control LacZ expression in predominantly migratory neural crest. This dual genetic approach that allows the authors to distinguish and compare pre-migratory and migratory neural crest cells is a strength of the work.

To assay for the differential expression of genes involved in the EMT and migration of cranial neural crest, the authors perform single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) using current methods. A strength is a large sample size per mouse line, and relatively high numbers of single cells analyzed. The authors identify six major cell/tissue types present in mouse E8.5 cranial tissues using known markers, which they then segregate into a cranial neural crest cluster using a well-reasoned bioinformatic strategy. The cranial neural crest cluster contains pre-migratory and migratory cells that they partition further into five subclusters and then characterize using the differential expression and combinatorial patterns of neural crest specifier genes, markers of pre-migratory neural crest, markers of early versus late migratory neural crest, markers of undifferentiated versus differentiated neural crest, tissue-specific markers, and region-specific markers. One weakness is that there is little attempt to map potential novel genes and/or pathways that also distinguish these clusters.

The authors then go on to subdivide the five cranial neural crest subclusters into almost two dozen smaller subclusters, again using the combinatorial expression of known markers (e.g., neural crest genes, cell junction genes, and cell cycle genes). A weakness is that the marker analysis and accompanying interpretation of the results relies heavily on the purported roles of different genes as described in the published work of others, which potentially introduces some untested assumptions and a bit of hand-waving into the study. Moreover, the limited correlation between mRNA and protein abundance for cell cycle markers is well documented in the literature but the authors rely heavily on gene expression to determine cell cycle status. Even though the authors add a compelling Edu/pHH3 double-labeling experiment and cell cycle inhibition studies, the work would be strengthened by including some analysis of protein expression to see if the cell cycle correlations hold up. Nonetheless, the subcluster and cell cycle analyses lead the authors to conclude that there are a series of intermediate cell states between neural crest EMT and delamination, and that cell cycle regulation is a defining feature and necessary component of those states. These novel findings are generally well supported by the data.

To test if there are spatiotemporal differences in the localization of neural crest cells during EMT in vivo, the authors apply a cutting-edge technique called signal amplification by exchange reaction for multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridization (SABER-FISH), which they validate using standard in situ hybridization. The authors select specific marker genes that seem justified based on their scRNA-seq dataset, and they generate a series of convincing images and quantitative data that add valuable depth to the story.

As a functional test of their hypothesis that one of the genes indicative of an EMT intermediate stage (i.e., Dlc1) is essential for neural crest migration, the authors use a lentivirus-mediated knockdown strategy. A strength is that the authors include appropriate scramble and cell death controls as part of their experimental design.

The authors use Sox10 as a marker to count neural crest cells, but Sox10 may only label a subset of neural crest cells and thus some unaffected lineages may not have been counted. Although the data are persuasive, a second marker for counting neural crest cells following knockdown would make the analysis more robust.

Overall, this is a first-rate study with many more strengths than weaknesses. The authors generate high quality data, and their interpretations are reasonable and balanced. Another strength is the writing, which is clear and well organized, and the figures (including supplemental), which are excellent and provide unambiguous visualization of some very complex data sets. The methods are state-of the art and are effectively executed, and they will be useful to the broader cell and developmental biology community. The work contains well-substantiated findings and supports the conclusion that EMT is a highly dynamic, multi-step process, which was previously thought to be more-or-less binary. Such findings will alter the way the field thinks about EMT in neural crest and the work will likely serve as an important example alongside cancer metastasis.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92844.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92844.3.sa3)

Summary:

Zhao et al. address the question of whether intermediate states of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) exist in a natural developmental context as well as in cancer cells. This is important not only for our understanding of these developmental systems but also for their development as resources for new anti-cancer approaches. Guided by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of delaminating mouse cranial neural crest cells, they identify two distinct populations with transcriptional signatures intermediate between neuroepithelial progenitors and migrating crest. Both clusters are also spatially intermediate and are actively cycling, with one in S-phase and one in G2/M. They show that blocking progression through S phase prior to the onset of delamination and knockdown of intermediate state marker Dlc1 both reduce the number of migratory cells that have completed EMT. Overall, the work provides a modern take and new insights into the classical developmental process of neural crest delamination.

Strengths:

• Deep analysis of the scRNAseq dataset revealed previously unappreciated cell populations intermediate between premigratory and migratory crest.

• The observation that delaminating/intermediate neural crest cells appear to be in S or G2/M phase is interesting and worth reporting, though the ultimate significance remains unclear, given that they do not make distinct derivatives depending on their cycle state.

• The authors employ new methods for multiplex spatial imaging to more accurately define their populations of interest and their relative positions.

• The authors present evidence that intermediate state gene Dlc1 (a Rho GAP) is not just a marker but functionally required for neural crest delamination in mouse, as previously shown in chicken.

Weaknesses:

• Similar experiments involving blockade of cell cycle progression and Dlc1 dose manipulation were previously performed in chick models, as noted in the discussion. The newly-defined intermediate states give added context to the results, but they are not entirely novel.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of E8.5 mouse embryos identified six major tissue types in cranial tissues, including cranial NCC, which were further subdivided into five subclusters. The final dataset consisted of 21,190 cells from two transgenic mouse lines (Wnt1-Cre;RosaLSL-eYFP and Mef2c-F10N-LacZ) that differentially label premigratory and migratory NCC populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C36 describe the experimental design, data collection, and initial clustering analysis. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate sample sizes (n=6 embryos per line), validated transgenic markers (C27-C29 with citations), and standard bioinformatic approaches. The identification of tissue types using established markers (C31-C35) is well-supported by Figure 1C-D.

results.result: Subclustering of cranial NCC revealed that subclusters 0-1 represent early migratory NCC expressing both migratory markers (Vim, Sox10, Twist1) and NCC specifier genes (Zeb2, Pax3, Nr6a1, Sox9, Foxd3, Snai1), while subclusters 2-3 represent late migratory NCC with higher expression of late migratory program genes. Subcluster 4 exhibits a neuroepithelial identity based on Sox1/Sox2 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with appropriate citations to established NCC markers. The inference that subclusters 0-1 represent earlier stages than 2-3 (C39) is logically derived from known biology of NCC specifier downregulation during migration. The characterization is consistent with published NCC development programs (C40).

results.result: Higher resolution clustering identified subcluster 17' as premigratory NCC based on high Wnt1 expression and expression of neural plate border/NCC specifier genes without migratory markers. Subclusters 2' and 10' were identified as EMT intermediate states, showing reduced Wnt1 and neural plate border specifiers compared to 17', along with decreased expression of tight junction/polarity genes and increased expression of cytoskeletal rearrangement genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by heatmap analysis in Figure 2D-E showing differential gene expression patterns. The identification of intermediate states is based on logical progression of marker expression (high Wnt1 → reduced Wnt1 → Sox10+) and molecular signatures consistent with EMT biology (junction breakdown, cytoskeletal changes). The inference is reasonable given the expression patterns, though the term 'intermediate' is interpretive.

results.result: The two intermediate NCC populations (subclusters 2' and 10') are distinguished by cell cycle phase, with 2' expressing S phase genes and 10' expressing G2/M phase genes. Pseudotime and trajectory analyses revealed that these populations form simultaneously and independently from premigratory NCC but converge into a common pool of early migratory NCC, suggesting NCC can undergo EMT and delamination in either S or G2/M phase without distinct downstream fates.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 are supported by cell cycle gene expression analysis (Figure 3A-B) and trajectory analysis (Figure 3C-D). The use of Monocle 3 for pseudotime analysis is appropriate. The interpretation that the two populations form independently but converge (C58-C59) is directly supported by the trajectory visualization. The inference about cell cycle-dependent delamination (C60) is reasonable but would benefit from additional validation beyond transcriptional data.

results.result: Cell cycle marker analysis revealed that the majority of delaminating cranial NCC express EdU (S phase) or pHH3 (G2/M phase) markers, while almost 50% of premigratory trunk NCC do not express either marker. This suggests that specific cell cycle phases are intimately connected to mouse cranial NCC EMT and delamination.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 4C-D (n=3 embryos). The comparison between cranial and trunk NCC is appropriate and reveals a meaningful difference. However, the inference in C64 is somewhat overstated—the data show correlation but not causation. The claim would be stronger if stated as 'associated with' rather than 'intimately connected to.'

results.result: Aphidicolin treatment to inhibit S phase cell cycle progression resulted in significantly fewer migratory NCC compared to controls, with minimal cell death. The remaining migratory NCC predominantly expressed pHH3 (G2/M marker), supporting that cranial NCC delamination in G2/M phase is independent of S phase delamination and demonstrating that cell cycle regulation is critical for cranial NCC delamination.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4B, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The Aphidicolin treatment successfully blocked S phase (no EdU incorporation) without inducing cell death (TUNEL staining). The significant reduction in migratory NCC (p<0.0001, n=3) and persistence of pHH3+ cells support the interpretation. However, the conclusion about 'independence' (C68) is inferential—the data show S phase inhibition doesn't completely block delamination, which is consistent with but doesn't definitively prove independence.

results.result: SABER-FISH spatial analysis revealed that intermediate stage NCC markers Dlc1, Sp5, and Pak3 are expressed in the dorsolateral region of the neuroepithelium, where Wnt1 expression is slightly diminished but Sox10 expression is minimal. This spatially resolves EMT intermediate stages to the dorsolateral edge of the neural plate border.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 are supported by SABER-FISH data in Figure 5B-C, including polyline kymograph analysis showing spatial expression gradients. The validation of SABER-FISH probes against traditional in situ hybridization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) strengthens confidence in the results. The spatial localization is clearly demonstrated and provides important in vivo validation of the scRNA-seq findings. The conclusion (C76) appropriately summarizes the spatial findings.

results.result: Dlc1 was prioritized for functional studies because it is highly expressed in all EMT intermediate stage NCC but not premigratory NCC, and Dlc1 null mice exhibit craniofacial malformations. Lentiviral shRNA knockdown of Dlc1 (achieving ~30% reduction) resulted in significantly fewer migratory NCC without affecting cell death, with all three shRNA constructs showing consistent effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C84 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6B-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The rationale for prioritizing Dlc1 is sound (C77-C80). The knockdown experiments show consistent, statistically significant reductions in migratory NCC across all three shRNA constructs (p<0.05 to p<0.0001, n=4 per group), with no increase in cell death (C83). However, the modest 30% knockdown level (C84) raises questions about whether this represents a physiologically relevant reduction or if the effect might be underestimated.

results.result: Dlc1 plays a critical role in regulating mouse cranial NCC delamination, potentially through its function as a Rho GTPase-activating protein that regulates Rho and Cdc42 activity, which in turn modulate actin cytoskeleton dynamics, stress fiber formation, filopodium formation, and tight junction organization.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 states a 'critical role' for Dlc1, which is supported by the knockdown data (C24, C81-C82). However, claims C85-C90 about the mechanism are largely speculative, based on citations to prior work on Dlc1 function rather than direct mechanistic studies in this system. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('may be mediated via,' C90), but the mechanistic claims remain unvalidated hypotheses requiring future work to test whether Dlc1 acts through RhoGTPase signaling in this context.

results.result: Studies in chicken and zebrafish embryos suggest that Dlc1 and related GAP family members regulate NCC delamination across vertebrate species, with Dlc1 overexpression causing ectopic delamination and loss of directionality, while Dlc1 inhibition reduces NCC emigration. This suggests the role of Dlc1 in NCC delamination might be evolutionarily conserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 appropriately summarize prior work in other species (with citations to Liu et al., 2017 and Clay and Halloran, 2013) and draw reasonable comparative conclusions. The speculation about evolutionary conservation (C98) is appropriately cautious ('might be'). However, these are not primary findings of this study but rather contextualization of the results within existing literature.

results.result: The identification of intermediate stage cranial NCC during delamination is consistent with NCC EMT being a developmental epithelial-to-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP) event. Similar to cancer EMT, NCC downregulate epithelial features while maintaining co-expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers and are localized at the dorsolateral edge. However, unlike some cancer intermediate states, mouse EMT intermediate NCC represent a transient state that eventually forms migratory NCC with mesenchymal character.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 represent the major conceptual conclusions of the study. The comparison to cancer EMP is supported by the data showing: (1) intermediate transcriptional states (C51-C53), (2) co-expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers (C52-C53, C108), (3) spatial localization at the tissue edge (C76, C109), and (4) transient nature with convergence to migratory state (C59, C110). The speculation about EMP being a common developmental phenomenon (C111) is appropriately cautious. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective findings.

results.result: Background claims establish that EMT is a cellular process converting epithelial to mesenchymal cells, traditionally viewed as binary but now recognized to involve intermediate states (EMP) in cancer. NCC formation represents a classic developmental EMT example, but whether intermediate states exist in developmental EMT remains largely unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent the current state of knowledge and properly motivate the study's research question (C12). No primary data evaluation is needed for these introductory claims.

results.result: During NCC formation, Sox1/Sox2 are downregulated in the dorsal neural plate border while Sox9/Sox10 are activated in the SoxB to SoxE switch. Overexpression studies show Sox2 represses NCC specification while Sox9/Sox10 promote NCC formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 summarize established knowledge about Sox gene regulation during NCC development, supported by multiple citations. These provide important context for interpreting the subcluster identities but are not primary findings of this study.

results.result: Cranial and trunk NCC exhibit differences in delamination timing (before vs. after neural plate closure), migration pattern (bulk collective vs. progressive chain migration), and regulatory networks, as established by prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 accurately summarize established differences between cranial and trunk NCC development, supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for the study's focus on cranial NCC and the comparative cell cycle analysis (C62-C63).

results.result: Prior studies in chicken and zebrafish embryos have shown that cell cycle status is associated with NCC delamination, with most trunk NCC in S phase during delamination, active cell division in dorsal neuroepithelium, and G1/S transition required for trunk NCC delamination. However, only ~30% of cranial NCC in chicken are in S phase during delamination.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C121 appropriately summarize prior work on cell cycle and NCC delamination in other species, supported by citations. These provide important comparative context for the mouse cranial NCC findings and highlight species/axial differences. The contrast with chicken cranial NCC (C119) is particularly relevant for interpreting the mouse results.

results.result: High DLC1 expression is detected in melanoma tissues, where it is necessary and sufficient for melanoma growth and metastasis, suggesting potential relevance to cancer biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 cite prior work (Yang et al., 2020b) connecting DLC1 to melanoma, which is relevant given that melanoma derives from neural crest. This provides translational context but is not a primary finding of the study.

results.result: Using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of E8.5 mouse embryos from two transgenic lines (Wnt1-Cre;RosaLSL-eYFP and Mef2c-F10N-LacZ), the authors identified two distinct intermediate NCC populations during EMT and delamination. These intermediate populations (subclusters 2' and 10') are distinguished by their cell cycle phase (S phase vs. G2/M phase), express unique transcriptional signatures including genes involved in cell protrusion (Dlc1, Pak3, Sp5), and show molecular features consistent with EMT (decreased cell junction genes, increased cytoskeletal rearrangement genes). Trajectory analysis revealed that these two intermediate populations form independently but converge into a common pool of early migratory NCC, suggesting they are not fate-restricted at this timepoint.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states 'Single-cell RNA seq data convincingly support what the authors claim. This is the first time to identify intermediate states between premigratory and migratory cranial NCCs.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The cranial neural crest cluster contains pre-migratory and migratory cells that they partition further into five subclusters...These novel findings are generally well supported by the data.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'Deep analysis of the scRNAseq dataset revealed previously unappreciated cell populations intermediate between premigratory and migratory crest.' The editor summarizes that the study reports 'compelling findings that intermediate states exist.'

results.result: The authors validated the cell cycle-dependent nature of NCC delamination through EdU/pHH3 double-labeling experiments showing that the majority of delaminating cranial NCC express cell cycle markers (EdU or pHH3 or both), while almost 50% of premigratory trunk NCC do not. Aphidicolin treatment to block S phase progression resulted in significantly fewer migratory NCC, with the remaining migratory NCC predominantly expressing pHH3 (G2/M marker), supporting the conclusion that cell cycle regulation is critical for cranial NCC delamination and that G2/M phase delamination is independent of S phase delamination.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 expresses concern about the reliance on mRNA expression for cell cycle determination: 'the limited correlation between mRNA and protein abundance for cell cycle markers is well documented in the literature but the authors rely heavily on gene expression to determine cell cycle status. Even though the authors add a compelling Edu/pHH3 double-labeling experiment and cell cycle inhibition studies, the work would be strengthened by including some analysis of protein expression to see if the cell cycle correlations hold up.' While the reviewer acknowledges the experiments are 'compelling,' they indicate the evidence would be stronger with additional protein-level validation. Reviewer 3 notes 'The observation that delaminating/intermediate neural crest cells appear to be in S or G2/M phase is interesting and worth reporting, though the ultimate significance remains unclear.'

results.result: Using SABER-FISH (signal amplification by exchange reaction for multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridization), the authors spatially localized the intermediate NCC populations to the dorsolateral region of the neuroepithelium. The intermediate stage markers Dlc1, Sp5, and Pak3 are highly expressed in the dorsolateral domain where Wnt1 expression is slightly diminished, while Sox10 (migratory marker) is minimally expressed in this transition region but highly expressed in more ventral migratory NCC.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms this work: 'To test if there are spatiotemporal differences in the localization of neural crest cells during EMT in vivo, the authors apply a cutting-edge technique called signal amplification by exchange reaction for multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridization (SABER-FISH), which they validate using standard in situ hybridization. The authors select specific marker genes that seem justified based on their scRNA-seq dataset, and they generate a series of convincing images and quantitative data that add valuable depth to the story.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors employ new methods for multiplex spatial imaging to more accurately define their populations of interest and their relative positions' as a strength.

results.result: Functional validation through lentivirus-mediated Dlc1 knockdown demonstrated that reducing Dlc1 expression by approximately 30% led to a significant reduction in the number of migratory NCC without affecting cell death, revealing a critical role for Dlc1 in regulating mouse cranial NCC delamination. Each of three different Dlc1 shRNA constructs produced significant reductions in migratory NCC compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Silencing one of the marker genes, Dlc1, reduces the migratory activity of cranial NCCs' as a strength. Reviewer 2 notes the experiments are well-designed with 'appropriate scramble and cell death controls' but raises a methodological concern: 'The authors use Sox10 as a marker to count neural crest cells, but Sox10 may only label a subset of neural crest cells and thus some unaffected lineages may not have been counted. Although the data are persuasive, a second marker for counting neural crest cells following knockdown would make the analysis more robust.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'The authors present evidence that intermediate state gene Dlc1 (a Rho GAP) is not just a marker but functionally required for neural crest delamination in mouse, as previously shown in chicken' but notes as a weakness that 'Similar experiments involving blockade of cell cycle progression and Dlc1 dose manipulation were previously performed in chick models...The newly-defined intermediate states give added context to the results, but they are not entirely novel.'

results.result: The authors conclude that their identification of intermediate stage cranial NCC during delamination is consistent with NCC EMT being a developmental epithelial-to-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP) event, similar to intermediate EMT states in cancer. Like cancer intermediate EMT states, NCC downregulate epithelial features while maintaining co-expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers, and intermediate stage NCC are localized at the dorsolateral edge of the neural plate border (analogous to the leading edge of tumors). However, unlike some cancer intermediate EMT cells, mouse EMT intermediate NCC represent a transient state that eventually forms migratory NCC with mesenchymal character.
results.evaluation: The editor's summary explicitly affirms this conclusion: 'This fundamental study reports compelling findings that intermediate states exist in epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) during natural development and differentiation of mammalian neural crest cells, similar to recent reports in cancer.' Reviewer 2 states 'The work contains well-substantiated findings and supports the conclusion that EMT is a highly dynamic, multi-step process, which was previously thought to be more-or-less binary. Such findings will alter the way the field thinks about EMT in neural crest and the work will likely serve as an important example alongside cancer metastasis.' Reviewer 1 notes 'These findings deepen our understanding of the mechanism of EMT in general.'

results.result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about EMT, including its role in development and cancer, the traditional binary view of EMT versus the more recent concept of epithelial-to-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP) with intermediate states in cancer, the similarities between developmental and cancer EMT, and the gap in knowledge regarding whether intermediate states exist in developmental EMT. Neural crest cells (NCC) are introduced as a classic example of developmental EMT.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these background claims. Reviewer 2 summarizes the rationale: 'During cancer progression, EMT seemingly includes cells at intermediate states as defined by the combinatorial expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers. But the importance of these markers and the role of these intermediate states remains unclear. Moreover, whether EMT during development also involves equivalent intermediate cell states is not known.' This framing is accepted by all reviewers as establishing the study's motivation.

results.result: The authors used established marker genes to identify and classify different cell populations in the scRNA-seq dataset, including Sox1/Sox2 for neural ectoderm, Cdh1 for non-neural ectoderm, eYFP/LacZ/Sox10/Twist for migrating NCC, Tbx1 for mesoderm, and Kdr for endothelial cells. They also identified region-specific markers (Dlx2 for pharyngeal arch, Alx1 for frontonasal mesenchyme) and discussed the SoxB to SoxE switch during NCC formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a methodological concern: 'A weakness is that the marker analysis and accompanying interpretation of the results relies heavily on the purported roles of different genes as described in the published work of others, which potentially introduces some untested assumptions and a bit of hand-waving into the study.' However, the reviewer also notes 'The authors identify six major cell/tissue types present in mouse E8.5 cranial tissues using known markers, which they then segregate into a cranial neural crest cluster using a well-reasoned bioinformatic strategy.' Another weakness noted is 'there is little attempt to map potential novel genes and/or pathways that also distinguish these clusters.' The reliance on known markers is both a strength (well-established) and weakness (potentially limiting).

results.result: The discussion contextualizes Dlc1 as a Rho GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that regulates RhoGTPases (Rho and Cdc42), which control cell morphology, motility, actin cytoskeleton, and tight junction organization. The authors cite previous work in chicken and zebrafish showing that Dlc1/Arhgap regulate NCC delamination and migration, suggesting the role of Dlc1 might be evolutionarily conserved in vertebrate embryos.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this context: 'The authors present evidence that intermediate state gene Dlc1 (a Rho GAP) is not just a marker but functionally required for neural crest delamination in mouse, as previously shown in chicken.' No reviewer challenges the mechanistic discussion or the evolutionary conservation argument, though Reviewer 3 notes the chicken experiments are not entirely novel.

results.result: The discussion places the findings in broader context by noting DLC1's role in melanoma, differences between cranial and trunk NCC delamination, and previous studies in chicken and zebrafish showing connections between cell cycle and NCC delamination. The authors note that while some studies showed cell cycle involvement in trunk NCC delamination, only about 30% of delaminating cranial NCC in chicken were in S phase, highlighting species and regional differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges this context: 'Similar experiments involving blockade of cell cycle progression and Dlc1 dose manipulation were previously performed in chick models, as noted in the discussion.' No reviewer challenges the accuracy of the cited literature or the comparative discussion, though Reviewer 3 notes this reduces the novelty of some findings.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on SABER-FISH spatial validation (C70-C76). Both evaluations find the spatial localization data convincing and well-supported. OpenEval notes validation against traditional in situ hybridization strengthens confidence; Peer reviewers explicitly praise the 'cutting-edge technique' and 'convincing images and quantitative data.'

Perfect agreement on background/introduction claims (C1-C17). Both evaluations accept these literature-based contextual claims as accurate and appropriate for motivating the study. No challenges raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on the major conceptual conclusion about intermediate EMT states (C107-C110). Both evaluations find this well-supported by the collective data. Peer reviewers explicitly state findings are 'compelling' and will 'alter the way the field thinks about EMT.' OpenEval notes conclusions are 'well-supported by the collective findings.'

Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, expressing concern about reliance on mRNA vs protein expression for cell cycle determination and requesting additional protein-level validation despite acknowledging experiments are 'compelling.'

Peer reviewers express similar concern about mRNA-protein correlation for cell cycle markers, requesting additional protein expression analysis.

Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting experiments are 'persuasive' but requesting a second marker beyond Sox10 for counting neural crest cells, and noting similar experiments were previously done in chicken.
